title: Quantum Anomaly Detection in network traffic using Variational Quantum Classifiers
authors: Mir H M Ilham, Hardique Dasore, Abdulrahman Ababneh, Hafidz A Kabira, Samyam Shrestha, Jeyasri Sundar, Shah Haque, Eric Howard
abstract: The increasingly complex cybersecurity landscape requires more advanced network anomaly detection systems. Although, classical machine learning models are known to be effective, they reach computational bottlenecks when processing high-dimensional data. This study investigates the potential of Quantum Machine Learning (QML) for network traffic anomaly detection by evaluating four distinct Variational Quantum Classifier (VQC) architectures. A synthetic network traffic dataset is generated for the evaluations. The VQC models systematically varied feature encoding methods, parameterized ansatz circuits, quantum neural network types, and classical optimizers. Experimental results show that a trade-off exists between circuit expressivity and optimization stability. Deeper circuits (VQC-4) achieved higher accuracy of upto 89.0\%, while simultaneously being sensitive to training conditions. A shallower variant (VQC-1) under performed, although it had consistent and stable optimization curves. Class-dependent biases were also observed such as in VQC-2, where the model struggled to find an effective decision boundary, and produced a large number of false negatives. The best performing model in this study (VQC-3) combined ZFeatureMap with RealAmplitudes ansatz, optimized using ADAM. Comparative analysis against classical machine learning models such as Support Vector Machine and Random Forest reveal a performance gap, where classical models are able to achieve perfect classification performance on the synthetic data. It is concluded that classical algorithms remain dominant in their ability to classify structured data with relatively simple class separations. However, due to the observed potential of certain VQC configurations to learn decision boundaries to classify data, their utility for future applications in noisier, higher-dimensional problems is highlighted.
summary: This paper investigates using Variational Quantum Classifiers (VQC) for network anomaly detection, benchmarking various quantum architectures against classical ML models. While the best VQC configuration showed promise, classical algorithms proved superior on the synthetic data due to its simple structure. The work highlights the potential of VQCs for more complex, noisy, high-dimensional problems in the future.
main_problem: Developing advanced network anomaly detection systems to handle high-dimensional data where classical machine learning models face computational bottlenecks.
main_result: Classical machine learning models significantly outperformed the tested Variational Quantum Classifiers (VQC) on synthetic data, achieving perfect classification.
method: The study systematically evaluated multiple VQC architectures by varying feature encoding, ansatz circuits, and optimizers, comparing them against classical baselines.
model_or_system: The core model is the Variational Quantum Classifier (VQC), a hybrid quantum-classical approach that maps classical data into a quantum state $|\psi(\mathbf{x}_i)angle$ manipulated by a parameterized unitary $U(	heta)$.
key_observables: Classification accuracy, F1-Score, optimization stability, and the performance gap compared to classical models.
important_parameters: Circuit depth (VQC-1 to VQC-4), feature encoding methods (e.g., ZFeatureMap), and optimization parameters (e.g., ADAM optimizer).
main_assumptions: The synthetic dataset used has low intrinsic complexity, allowing classical models to achieve perfect separation, and the study operates within the constraints of the NISQ era.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the methodology flow, feature distributions (showing correlation), and PCA visualizations showing cluster separation between normal and anomalous traffic.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem, details the VQC methodology (data preprocessing, quantum encoding, hybrid training), presents systematic comparative results across different VQC architectures, and concludes with a discussion on future potential.
why_interesting: It applies quantum machine learning techniques (VQC) to a real-world data problem (cybersecurity), providing a structured benchmark of quantum advantage in a domain relevant to quantum information processing.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The methodology overview illustrates the pipeline steps of data generation, preprocessing, quantum feature encoding, hybrid quantum-classical training, and model evaluation.
Figure 2: The feature distribution plot visualizes both individual feature distributions (diagonal subplots) and pairwise relationships between features in a grid format.

Figure 3: Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was applied to project the dataset features into a two dimensional space. It is a statistical dimensionality reduction technique that transforms the data while preserving maximum possible variance.
Figure 4: A feature correlation heatmap visualizes correlation among variables in the data. In this case, it can be observed that strong positive relationships exist among all features.
Figure 5: VQC-1 feature encoding using the ZZFeatureMap maps classical input features into a quantum state by applying both single-qubit rotations and entangling operations.
